title: Modern Red & Purple Teaming Excellence
description: Excellence in adversarial simulation: moving from point-in-time pentests to continuous, collaborative validation. Covers agentic AI, identity-centric attacks, and open-book purple teaming.

modules.title: The Foundations of Excellence
modules.objective: Understand the strategic difference between penetration testing, red teaming, and purple teaming, and learn how to properly prepare and scope an engagement for maximum business value.

topics.title: Beyond Pentesting: Red vs. Pentest vs. Purple
concepts: Penetration Testing: Point-in-time assessment focused on finding as many vulnerabilities as possible.
Red Teaming: Goal-oriented adversarial simulation focusing on testing detection and response capabilities (the SOC/Blue Team).
Purple Teaming: Collaborative, open-book exercise where red and blue work together to validate and tune detections in real-time.
Testing the triad: People, Process, and Technology, rather than just technical flaws.
key_facts: A penetration test finds flaws; a red team engagement tests the organization's resilience and incident response.
Excellent red teaming focuses on emulation of specific, relevant threat actors (TTPs) rather than ad-hoc exploitation.
Purple teaming is iterative and aims to replace assumptions about security posture with data.

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Blue teams should experience a red team engagement exactly as a real attack, testing their full incident response playbook.

drills: Draft a comparative table showing the goals, scope, and deliverables of a pentest vs a red team engagement.
Identify an appropriate scenario where a company should choose a purple team exercise over a red team engagement.
common_mistakes: Treating a red team engagement as an extended penetration test.
Focusing only on 'winning' (getting Domain Admin) rather than measuring how long it takes to be detected.

topics.title: Strategic Preparation & Rules of Engagement
concepts: Defining clear, actionable objectives (flags) based on real-world business risks.
Rules of Engagement (RoE): Documenting scope, off-limits assets, and emergency escalation paths.
White Cell oversight: The control team that monitors the engagement, ensures safety, and provides 'leg ups' if needed.
Executive Buy-in: Ensuring stakeholders are aligned while keeping the broader organization unaware to maintain realism.
key_facts: Success is determined during the planning phase, not just execution.
The White Cell acts as a referee, ensuring the red team stays in scope and the blue team is tested fairly.
Explicit RoE prevents accidental service disruption and ensures legal authorization.

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Ideally, nothing out of the ordinary until the red team begins execution. If discovered early, the White Cell manages communication.

drills: Design a realistic 'flag' for a financial institution that goes beyond simple network access.
Draft a White Cell escalation matrix for a scenario where a production database goes offline during testing.
common_mistakes: Setting generic goals like 'test our security' instead of specific, measurable objectives.
Failing to establish a dedicated, out-of-band communication channel for the White and Red cells.

modules.title: Modern Adversary TTPs & Engineering
modules.objective: Explore how modern adversaries operate, focusing on identity-centric attacks and the emerging use of AI and automation in red teaming.

topics.title: Identity-Centric Attacks
concepts: Shift from exploiting software vulnerabilities to compromising identities and access.
OAuth token abuse, consent phishing, and SSO (Single Sign-On) manipulation.
Cloud IAM (Identity and Access Management) escalation and misconfigurations.
Human-in-the-loop exploitation (e.g., social engineering helpdesks for MFA resets).
key_facts: Modern breaches frequently start with identity compromise rather than zero-day exploits.
Adversaries target the trust relationships between cloud services, exploiting excessive IAM permissions.
Helpdesks are prime targets for social engineering to bypass strong authentication.

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Authentication logs showing anomalous access patterns, impossible travel, or unusual OAuth consent grants.

drills: Analyze a scenario where an attacker uses consent phishing to gain access to a user's Office 365 mailbox.
Map out the attack path for a helpdesk social engineering attack leading to a full domain compromise.
common_mistakes: Relying solely on MFA without considering MFA bypass techniques like AiTM (Adversary-in-the-Middle) or fatigue attacks.
Ignoring third-party application permissions in cloud environments.

topics.title: Agentic AI & Automated Red Teaming
concepts: Agentic AI: Autonomous software agents capable of reasoning, planning, and executing attack paths without human intervention.
Continuous Automated Red Teaming (CART): Integrating red team testing into CI/CD pipelines for continuous validation.
Automated Progressive Red Teaming (APRT): Adapting strategies over time to test AI models against advanced threats like multi-turn jailbreaks.
Adversarial Machine Learning: Techniques like context poisoning and prompt injection.
key_facts: CART allows organizations to validate defenses continuously as their environment changes, rather than annually.
Agentic AI can rapidly explore complex attack graphs that would take human operators significantly longer.
Securing LLMs requires automated progressive testing to handle evolving jailbreak techniques.

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Continuous, low-level probing that mimics automated scanning or agentic behavior, often focused on newly deployed assets.
detections: Detection of known prompt injection patterns

drills: Compare the benefits of a CART platform versus a traditional quarterly penetration test.
Develop a basic prompt injection payload to test an LLM's guardrails.
common_mistakes: Replacing human red teams entirely with automated tools; automation handles breadth, humans handle depth and novel paths.
Deploying CART without fine-tuning, leading to alert fatigue for the SOC.

modules.title: Purple Teaming & Exposure Validation
modules.objective: Master the collaborative approach of purple teaming to iteratively improve detection engineering and validate security controls.

topics.title: The Purple Team Paradigm
concepts: Open-book collaboration: Red and blue teams sitting together (virtually or physically) during the execution of attacks.
Replacing assumptions with data: Validating if existing security controls actually stop or detect specific behaviors.
Focus on TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) rather than just IOCs (Indicators of Compromise).
Fostering a culture of learning and continuous improvement between offensive and defensive teams.
key_facts: Purple teaming is an exercise type, not a separate team.
The primary outcome is improved resilience and tuned detections, not just a list of vulnerabilities.
It bridges the communication gap that often exists after traditional red team engagements.

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Blue team actively monitors their SIEM and EDR while the red team executes, correlating actions to telemetry in real-time.

drills: Outline an agenda for a one-day purple team exercise focusing on lateral movement techniques.
Describe how to handle a scenario where a red team technique generates no telemetry on the blue team's side.
common_mistakes: Conducting the exercise adversarially (trying to 'beat' the other team) instead of collaboratively.
Failing to capture and document the exact telemetry generated by each executed technique.

topics.title: Iterative Detection Tuning & Telemetry
concepts: The feedback loop: Execute technique -> Check telemetry -> Check detection -> Tune rule -> Re-execute.
Mapping coverage using the MITRE ATT&CK framework (e.g., ATT&CK Navigator).
Identifying telemetry gaps (blind spots) vs. detection gaps (data exists, but no alert).
Writing and deploying Sigma rules or specific SIEM queries based on the purple team findings.
key_facts: A missing detection is often a telemetry problem (the right logs aren't being collected).
Tuning reduces false positives and ensures high-fidelity alerts for the SOC.
Iterative testing proves that a newly written detection rule actually works against the specific attack tool.

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: The evolution of an alert from non-existent, to noisy, to highly tuned and actionable.
detections: Newly created or refined Sigma rules

drills: Write a simple detection rule for a simulated attack technique and describe the process of tuning it to reduce false positives.
Use the ATT&CK Navigator to visually represent the improvement in detection coverage after a purple team exercise.
common_mistakes: Tuning detections based only on the specific tool the red team used, rather than the underlying behavior.
Not re-testing the technique after the detection rule has been implemented.
